title: The Anthropic IPO Concerns Me
content:
Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public in what became the largest IPO in American history. Given my sustained criticism of Anthropic’s beliefs and actions, many people have asked me for my opinion on this event.
The good news for the curious among you is that I captured my thoughts in an op-ed for The New York Times, which they published Thursday, the same day that Anthropic went public. It was titled “Don’t Play Anthropic’s Game,” and it opens as follows:
“By the close of the stock market today, Anthropic will have become a central pillar of the American economy. This is deeply concerning to me, because it’s unclear how many of the retail and institutional investors handing over their money to Anthropic realize that they are, in some sense, funding a doomsday cult that also happens to build enterprise software.”
My use of “doomsday cult” isn’t facetious; it underscores a critical reality. As many have reported (including myself), the leaders of Anthropic have long believed that AI is destined to transform the human species, either delivering a utopia or killing us all. They see themselves, with their highly rational minds, trained on long hours during the 2000s debating these issues on blogs like Less Wrong and Overcoming Bias, as the select few who must rise up to guide humanity through this next evolution.
This may sound like hyperbole, but it’s not. It’s exactly what they believe.
Some ask, “Why is this a problem? If any company is going to advance AI, shouldn’t it be one that cares about bad outcomes?”
As I elaborate in my op-ed, the situation is not so simple. Anthropic’s belief that transformational AI is imminent has made it reckless. Anthropic now releases models faster than they can build safeguards because they believe the fate of the human race depends on getting to superintelligent AI first. (Case in point: earlier this year, they announced they were relaxing rules that required them to slow down development if models became hard to control. Their reason? If they applied such rules “unilaterally,” other – presumably less righteous – parties might get ahead of them in the race.)
Indeed, Anthropic stated a key rationale for their IPO is to raise the money needed to accelerate investments in so-called “recursive self-improvement,” where AI systems upgrade themselves. This is, of course, a terrible idea, as it creates models that are even less safe and harder to understand. Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its S-1 filing, but sees no alternative if they’re to continue as humanity’s shepherd through this revolution.
It’s unclear to what degree they even care about profits or building a durable business. As I summarize in my op-ed:
“It’s a business plan that starts with a lot of red ink and then abruptly ends with superintelligence arriving and rendering money superfluous.”
To be clear: generative AI is an incredibly important technological revolution. It brings with it great promises and real risks. But the right way to navigate these innovations can’t possibly be to let a small number of people in Silicon Valley, who have been worshipping AI as a millenarian agent since well before LLMs entered the scene, gather as much money as possible to fund their self-proclaimed role as prophets who will lead the rest of us to their idiosyncratic vision of a better future.
In Other News
For more on the question of whether Amodei and company are right in their beliefs that we’re on a trajectory toward superintelligence, check out my recent technical article for the IEEE Spectrum, which lays out an engineering case against the feasibility of AI superintelligence. (You should also consider signing up for the Spectrum’s always insightful AI Alert newsletter.)

report.summary: Cal Newport warns that Anthropic's record-setting IPO funnels public money into a company whose leaders see themselves as shepherds through an AI doomsday-or-utopia transition, pushing speed over safety.
report.background: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers, many with roots in the effective-altruism and rationalist communities that gathered on blogs like Less Wrong and Overcoming Bias. From the start it positioned itself as the safety-focused frontier lab, betting that being at the cutting edge was the only credible way to steer AI. But frontier training costs billions per year, and the competitive race with OpenAI and Google has repeatedly forced the company to trade caution for speed. Newport, a computer scientist and author who has been critical of the rationalist worldview, published a New York Times op-ed the same day as the listing, arguing that investors underestimate what they are actually funding: a mission-driven project whose stated goal is superintelligence, not a conventional enterprise-software business.
key_points: Newport calls Anthropic's leadership a 'doomsday cult' in earnest, not as insult. He argues they genuinely believe AI will either produce utopia or kill everyone, and that they are the rational few who must guide humanity through it. Investors buying shares, in his view, may not grasp how much that worldview shapes company decisions.

The safety argument cuts both ways. Anthropic has relaxed internal rules that would slow development when models become hard to control, reasoning that unilateral restraint lets less careful competitors get ahead. Newport sees this as proof that belief in imminent superintelligence produces recklessness, not caution.

A stated rationale for the IPO is funding 'recursive self-improvement', where AI systems upgrade themselves. Newport calls this obviously dangerous, since it makes models less safe and harder to understand. Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its S-1 filing but argued it had no alternative path.

The business model is unusual. Newport summarizes it as a plan that starts with heavy losses and ends abruptly when superintelligence arrives and makes money irrelevant, suggesting ordinary profitability is not the organizing goal.
report.impact: For the AI industry, an Anthropic listing of this scale would set a benchmark valuation for safety-branded labs, likely pulling more private capital into frontier training and reinforcing the race dynamic Newport criticizes. It also mainstreams the idea that superintelligence is an imminent engineering target rather than a speculative horizon, which shapes hiring, regulation and investor expectations. For developers, the practical consequence is more capable APIs and faster release cadences, but also less predictable model behavior, shorter deprecation cycles and safety documentation that lags the product. For regular users, AI becomes embedded in everyday infrastructure backed by a company whose stated priorities are not customer profitability; the risk is not a Hollywood takeover but governance that is opaque, hard to contest and driven by a narrow ideological frame.
report.tools: Readers who want to follow the underlying debate can track Anthropic's S-1 filing for stated risk factors, and subscribe to IEEE Spectrum's AI Alert newsletter, where Newport makes an engineering case against near-term superintelligence. For hands-on safety work, look at open-source interpretability tooling such as TransformerLens and SAELens, plus evaluation frameworks like EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness. Reading Less Wrong and Overcoming Bias directly gives useful context on the worldview officials are acting on.
